## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to compose shifts and OR to implement rotate without loops or conditionals, a common low-level operation.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise shifts and wrap-around semantics
- 32-bit boundary, undefined behavior avoidance
- Performance and portability considerations

## Code Example

```javascript
function rotl32(n, k) {
  return ((n << k) | (n >>> (32 - k))) >>> 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- What happens if k === 0? How does the expression evaluate?
- How would you implement rotate-right similarly?
- How would you adapt for 64-bit values in a language without native unsigned support?

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to reason about 128-bit bit patterns and leverage existing helper functions to implement non-trivial properties without using conditional branches.

## Key Concepts
- Bit reversal and palindrome detection in 128-bit space
- Constant-time, branchless implementation

int isPalindrome128(uint64_t hi, uint64_t lo) {

  reverse128(hi, lo, &rhi, &rlo);
  return (rhi == hi && rlo == lo);

- What optimizations could be applied if the function were called frequently?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to apply simple bit-tricks succinctly and reason about edge cases without loops. It also shows understanding of bitwise adjacency relationships across 64 bits.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise AND and right shift
- Detecting pattern overlap without branching
- Constant-time evaluation on fixed width integers

## Code Example

```javascript
function hasConsecutiveOnes(n) {
  // n treated as a 64-bit value; bitwise ops apply to 32-bit in JS
  return (n & (n >>> 1)) !== 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you extend to count how many adjacent pairs exist?
- How would you test correctness with edge inputs like all zeros, all ones, alternating patterns?
